study.title: Joshua 22 - Unity, Zeal and the altar as a testimony
study.overview: Joshua 22 narrates the farewell of the eastern Jordan tribes and a serious misunderstanding that almost ends in civil war between Israelites. The chapter shows Joshua exhorting to allegiance to the Lord before sending these tribes back to their lands; then he presents the construction of an altar that alarms the other tribes, because it seems to threaten the central worship of the Lord. The crisis is resolved through careful investigation, a clear defense of the accused and the restoration of peace. The outcome highlights that the altar would not be used for sacrifice, but as a testimony that the Lord is God and that the tribes east and west of the Jordan belonged to the same covenant people.

outline.title: Joshua fires and admonishes the Eastern tribes
outline.explanation: Joshua recognizes the obedience of the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half tribe of Manasseh, recalls his allegiance in support of the other Israelites and sends them back with blessing. The farewell includes a decisive call to continuous obedience: to love the Lord, to walk in his ways and to serve him with all his heart and with the whole soul.

outline.title: An altar raises suspicion of rebellion
outline.explanation: As they reach the Jordan, the Eastern tribes build an altar of great appearance. The western tribes interpret the act as a threat to the unity of worship and prepare war, recalling previous episodes of community judgment, such as Peor's transgression and Achan's guilt. Before attacking, they send Fineias and ten leaders to figure out the case.

outline.title: Eastern tribes explain the purpose of the altar
outline.explanation: The Eastern tribes deny any rebellion and claim that the altar was not made for burnt offerings or sacrifices. Their fear was that in the future the children of the west would tell their descendants that they had no part in the Lord. The altar would be a visible witness of belonging common to the Lord, and not a rival of the altar before the tabernacle.

outline.title: Peace is restored and the altar is named
outline.explanation: Fineties and the leaders are satisfied with the explanation and recognize that the Lord was among the people. The congregation blesses God and gives up war. Finally, the Eastern tribes set the altar Eof, that is, testimony, to declare that the Lord is God.

study.context: The chapter is situated in the period when Israel had already completed the conquest and division of the land, but it still needed to consolidate the lives of the people under the covenant. The notes highlight that Joshua is in his final farewells and that the focus of the book is to convey to religious fidelity posterity, not just register customs or political organization. It is also clear that the concern of the western tribes with the altar relates to the integrity of God-ordained worship, in contrast to practices that could be seen as rebellion.
study.theology: Joshua 22 teaches that the unity of God's people depends on faithfulness to the Lord and obedience to his commandment, not only of geographical proximity or ethnic ties. The chapter values the zeal for the holiness of worship, but it also requires prudence: before condemning, one must listen and examine. There is a healthy tension between zeal and discernment. The altar is not celebrated as a religious innovation, but as a memorial that protects communion and recalls that the identity of the people comes from the Lord. The final verse interprets the altar as a testimony, showing that the true security of Israel is in publicly confessing that the Lord is God. The narrative also warns that the sin of an individual or a group can have consequences for the whole community, as suggested by references to Peor and Achan.

scholarViews.insight: The Repetition The Lord... is God" shows the shock of the Eastern tribes in the face of the accusation of rebellion; his response emphasizes that the intention of the altar was a witness, not idolatrous.
Joshua records this farewell to inculcate in posterity the sense of religion and duty to God, rather than to satisfy historical curiosities.
The Western tribes did not want to act rashly; so they sent Fineias and ten leaders to clarify the intention of the altar before warring.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the difference between a holy zeal and a precipitated accusation against other brothers in the faith?
In what ways can a public memorial serve spiritual fidelity without replacing worship due to God alone?
How does continuing obedience, highlighted by Joshua, protect the community from future crises?
study.practice: This text calls the church and every believer to unite doctrinal fidelity with humility in dealing with brothers and sisters. Before concluding that someone is in error, one needs to listen, investigate and seek clarity. At the same time, the passage reminds us that commitments with God are not only personal: our actions can strengthen or hurt the communion of the people. In practice, it is worth cultivating a life of persevering obedience, words that promote peace and visible signs that point to the Lord, without competing with the worship that belongs only to him.
study.uncertainty: Adam Clarke's note on the name of the altar indicates that the word corresponding to 'witness' appears in some ancient texts and versions, while in others it is understood as part of the name itself; therefore, it is not possible to affirm with absolute certainty the exact form of the term in the base text only from the given notes. In addition, Matthew Henry's quote provided is partial, but sufficient to support the included pointing.
